sceneHappening: Treating different groups in the church: older and younger, widows, and elders; some advice for Timothy himself
summary: Timothy is not to rebuke an older man "but exhort him as a father; the younger men as brothers; the elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, in all purity." "Honor widows who are widows indeed." If a widow has children or grandchildren, "let them learn first to show piety toward their own family and to repay their parents, for this is acceptable in the sight of God." The widow "indeed and desolate" has her hope on God and "continues in petitions and prayers night and day," while one who lives for pleasure "is dead while she lives." "If anyone doesn't provide for his own, and especially his own household, he has denied the faith, and is worse than an unbeliever." Rules for the widows' list: "Let no one be enrolled as a widow under sixty years old, having been the wife of one man, being approved by good works," such as raising children, hospitality, "washed the saints' feet," relieving the afflicted. Younger widows are to be refused, because they may "grow wanton against Christ" and desire to marry, and may learn to be "idle, going about from house to house... gossips and busybodies"; Paul wants them to "marry, bear children, rule the household, and give no occasion to the adversary for insulting," because some have already "turned away after Satan." Believers with widows in the family should relieve them, "and don't let the assembly be burdened." Elders "who rule well" are "worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in the word and in teaching," quoting "You shall not muzzle the ox when it treads out the grain" and "The laborer is worthy of his wages." An accusation against an elder needs "two or three witnesses"; those who sin are to be reproved "in the sight of all." Timothy is to act "without prejudice, doing nothing by partiality," to "lay hands hastily on no one," and to keep himself pure. "Be no longer a drinker of water only, but use a little wine for your stomach's sake and your frequent infirmities." Some men's sins and some good works are obvious; others show later.
whySettingMatters: Widows in the ancient world had no pension or social safety net; a widow without family could starve, so the church's care for them (Acts 6:1-6) was a practical help. This chapter separates three groups: widows with family, who should be cared for by their relatives; widows truly alone, who are supported by the church; and younger widows, who are encouraged to remarry. The "enrolled" widows (5:9) were probably a formal list for support, perhaps with some duty of prayer and service; the age of sixty and the phrase "wife of one man" are conditions of the list, and scholars disagree on whether it was an order or office or simply a care list. The harsh sound of 5:11-15 reflects a worry about the church's reputation and about idle talk, and also gives a rule for the particular situation in Ephesus ("some have already turned away after Satan"). "Double honor" in 5:17 uses a word (timē) that can mean respect, or payment, or both; the two quotations in 5:18 point toward pay, and Paul cites Deuteronomy 25:4 in the same way in 1 Corinthians 9:9. The rule of two or three witnesses comes from Deuteronomy 19:15. "Lay hands hastily on no one" (5:22) may refer to appointing leaders or to restoring those who had been disciplined; it is not clear which. The little verse about wine in 5:23 is the only personal medical comment in the letter; it shows both that Timothy was in the habit of avoiding wine, perhaps because of the false teachers' rules (4:3), and that Paul treats it as a practical matter.

people.note: Gives practical rules for the church's care of different groups.
Told to treat each group like family, and to take a little wine for his stomach.
Cared for by the family first, then by the church.
Worthy of double honor; accusations need witnesses.

questions: Paul starts by saying to treat each person in the church like family. How would that change the way you correct someone older or younger than you?
The chapter puts the first duty of caring for a widow on her family. What do you notice about how the church and the family share the load?
Paul asks for "double honor" for elders who work at teaching. What does it look like to honor those who serve the church in a way that is real and not just polite?
The advice about wine for Timothy's stomach sits in the middle of serious instructions. Why might Paul include it?
